newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Berisha to quit as left prepares to rule.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Berisha to quit as left prepares to rule.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha said on Wednesday he would resign when a leftist government took power, but tried to ensure his defeated Democratic Party stayed in control of security forces at least temporarily.

The Socialist Party has claimed victory in the first round of last Sunday's general election and partial results showed they could be heading for a landslide win. Berisha conceded the defeat of his Democrats less than 24 hours after polls closed. A second round takes place on July 6.
Berisha, holding his first news conference since the election, said he expected the Socialists, reformed heirs of the communist party, to lead Albania's new administration.
Pressed repeatedly on whether he would therefore resign, the president, in power since 1992, said in English:
"Definitely. There is no doubt of that. I never had the smallest doubt in that respect."

Berisha stressed that he had his duties to perform before the next government was formed, suggesting he would hand in his resignation once the new parliament convened. Under the constitution, parliament elects and removes the head of state.
In Tirana's central Skanderbeg Square, Socialist leaders held a peaceful rally ahead of Sunday's second round run-offs which turned into an early victory celebration.
Socialist leader Fatos Nano, released in March after spending three years in jail following a suspect trial, addressed a crowd of around 7,000 people, waving Albanian and Socialist party flags.

"First Berisha stole your votes and then he stole your money," Nano said in reference to last year's disputed general election and the collapse of pyramid investment schemes early this year. Thousands of Albanians lost their savings.

"We are going to turn Albania into a modern country to face the challenges of the future. Not Berisha's primitive capitalism, but a real market system with private banks and a strong currency, free of corruption," he added.
Nano said a leftist government would be ready to work with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank and abide by the advice they gave in ordering the country's finances.

"Experience shows that any delay in implementing reforms brings only corruption, ignorance and destruction to the economy," he said, flanked by fellow Socialist and interim Prime Minister Bashkim Fino.

Partial results issued by the central electoral commission after the count in 75 of 115 constituencies were complete showed the Socialists and their allies had won 45 seats and Berisha's Democrats eight. No candidate won an outright majority in 22 other seats which will be decided in a second round on Sunday.
In 40 seats contested under a proportional system, the Socialists scored 52.18 percent and the Democrats 26.09.
While the country awaited final results, Berisha and Fino were involved in a power struggle over the control of security forces and in particular over the post of interior minister.
Under a state of emergency introduced on March 2 and still in force, the interior ministry controls not only the police but also the armed forces and secret police.
The post was assigned to Berisha's Democratic Party in a deal signed by 10 parties in March setting up an interim government ahead of the early elections.
The presidential office insisted on Wednesday evening that the post was vacant because Interior Minister Belul Celo had left the country. Fino said Celo was still in office.
"The minister should be urgently replaced as he was the commander of operations under the state of emergency," Albanian television said, quoting a statement by the president's office.
Control of the security forces is considered vital in a country slowly emerging from 45 years of Stalinist rule, ended by a popular revolt in 1990.
